title: A ring buffer
objectives: Build a fixed-size single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer.

screens.title: Fill a ring of four
screens.prose: A ring is a fixed row of slots. Items come out at the head and go in at the tail. Step through five pushes, 1 to 5, then pops until it is empty.

state.caption: An empty ring of 4. The head and tail counters both read 0.

frames.caption: An empty ring of 4. The head and tail counters both read 0.
push 5 is refused: the ring is full, tail - head = 4.
pop finds the ring empty: head equals tail.

screens.question: Answer both: which push is refused, and what does the third pop return?

rows: What does the third pop return?

hints.text: Step to the end of the pushes and read the captions.
Four slots hold four items, so one push too many is refused.
The fifth push is refused. Pops come out in the order pushed, so the third pop returns 3.

feedback.correct: The fifth push is refused, and the third pop returns 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step through and read each caption.

byKey.r0c1: The ring has four slots, so only the fifth push has no room.
byKey.r1c1: Pops return items in the order they were pushed: 1, 2, 3, 4.

explain.text: Four slots take pushes 1 to 4, and the fifth finds the ring full. Pops return 1, 2, 3 and 4 in order, and a fifth pop finds it empty. Full is a tail four ahead of the head, empty is equal counters.

screens.title: From counter to slot
screens.prose: The two counters only ever grow. The slot an item uses is the counter reduced to the ring size. A ring of 8 has head 13 and tail 20. Neither counter has been reset.

state.caption: A ring of 8. Head counter 13, tail counter 20.

screens.question: Fill in the ring.

rows: Slot of counter 5 in a ring of 4

hints.text: A ring of 4 has slots 0 to 3, so counter 5 wraps once.
Items stored is the tail minus the head. A ring of 8 has slots 0 to 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Counter 5 is one past a full lap of 4, so slot 1.
byKey.r1c1: $20 - 13$ items sit between the head and the tail.

explain.text: A counter maps to slot counter mod N, and for a power of two that is `counter & (N - 1)`. The size is tail minus head, 7, so one slot is still free. The next push goes to 20 & 7 = 4, just before the head's slot 5.

screens.title: When the counters wrap
screens.prose: An `unsigned` counter wraps to 0 after 4,294,967,295. Here the tail passes the wrap, with the head two behind. A `size_t` is 4 bytes in this app and 8 on a desktop, so the listing uses `unsigned`.
screens.question: Fill in the slots, and how long a wrap takes.

rows: Seconds until a counter wraps at 10 million pushes a second

hints.text: A power of two divides $2^{32}$ evenly, so the low bits carry on.
$2^{32} \bmod 3 = 1$, so a ring of 3 breaks at the wrap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: 4,294,967,292 is a multiple of 4, so 293 sits in slot 1.
byKey.r1c1: 4,294,967,295 is 3 × 1,431,655,765, so it leaves no remainder.

explain.text: A power-of-two ring keeps slot order across the wrap: 2, 3, 0, 1, and tail minus head stays 2. A ring of 3 puts counters 4,294,967,295 and 0 in the same slot, because $2^{32}$ leaves remainder 1. At 10 million pushes a second the wrap comes after 429.5 s, so it will happen.

screens.title: Two counters, one line
screens.prose: The producer writes `tail_` and the consumer writes `head_`, on two cores. A cache line is 64 bytes, shown as 8 words of 8 bytes. A core that writes a word takes the whole line from the other core.
screens.question: Tap every word that moves to the producer's core when it stores `tail_`.

hints.text: Which unit does a cache move between cores?
A core takes a whole line, not one word.
All eight words of line 1 move, including `head`.

feedback.correct: The whole line: all eight words, including `head`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A cache moves lines, not words.

byKey.r1c6: You tapped only `tail`. The line travels as one 64-byte unit.
byKey.r1c5: The `head` word moves too, because it shares the line.
byKey.r2c1: Line 2 is empty here. It does not move.

explain.text: Cores exchange whole 64-byte lines, so a store to `tail_` pulls `head_` along. The consumer's next store to `head_` pulls the line back. Neither counter is shared, yet the line ping-pongs: false sharing.

screens.title: What the line costs
screens.prose: A store that steals the line costs about 60 ns, and 1 ns when the line stays put. Say `alignas(64)` gives each counter a line of its own. The producer pushes 10 million items a second.
screens.question: Fill in the stall each second.

rows: Both counters on one line (60 ns a push)
Each counter on its own line (1 ns a push)

hints.text: Ten million pushes, each paying the cost.
$10^7 \times 60$ ns, then change nanoseconds to milliseconds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the pushes a second by the cost of one.

explain.text: Stealing the line costs 600 ms of every second, 60% of a core, for a correct queue. With `alignas(64)` each counter keeps its own line and the cost falls to 10 ms. The test in the next task compares the two addresses.

screens.title: The producer's push
screens.prose: Level 2 gave the memory orders. A `release` store publishes everything written before it, and an `acquire` load sees it. The producer owns `tail_` and only reads `head_`. Put the producer's push in order. Leave out the lines that do not belong.

lines: T buf_[N];   // N a power of two
bool push(const T& v);   // producer only
params.title: The ring

screens.question: Order the lines of `push`.

lines.why: A relaxed store can become visible before the slot write, so the consumer could read a stale slot.
Only the consumer writes `head_`. A second writer would race with it.
Each counter has one writer, so no lock is needed.

hints.text: Check for room, write the item, then publish.
The tail must change only after the slot holds the value.
Load the tail, check space against the head, write the slot, store the tail with `release`, return true.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first marked line.

byKey.left-out: Every one of the five kept lines is needed.
byKey.s3: The slot write must come before the tail store, or the consumer sees an item not there yet.
byKey.s4: Publishing the tail before the slot is written lets the consumer read an empty slot.

explain.text: The producer reads its own `tail_` relaxed, checks `head_` with `acquire`, and writes the slot. The `release` store of `tail_ + 1` publishes the slot write, so the consumer's `acquire` load of the tail sees it. A relaxed store would not order the two.

screens.title: Does it need a lock
screens.prose: Two threads share the ring: one pushes and one pops. A colleague wants a mutex around both calls to be safe.

lines: producer: writes buf_[t & mask], then tail_
consumer: reads buf_[h & mask], then head_
params.title: Who writes what

screens.question: Does this ring need a mutex?

options.text: No: each counter has one writer
Yes: both threads write the buffer
options.why: They write different slots. The counters hand each slot from one thread to the other.
A vector is not thread safe. The ring needs no lock for a different reason.
The consumer does not share a counter with another writer, so it needs no lock either.

hints.text: Who writes `tail_`? Who writes `head_`?
Each counter has exactly one writer.
The slots are written by one thread and read by the other, and the counters order those accesses.

feedback.correct: No lock for one producer and one consumer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the writers of each variable.

byKey.yes: You said both threads write the buffer. They write different slots.
byKey.vector: A vector gives no such promise. The ring is safe because of its counters.
byKey.pop: `pop` writes only `head_`, which nobody else writes.

explain.text: A race needs two writers of one variable. The producer alone writes `tail_` and its slots, and the consumer alone writes `head_`. A release and acquire pair makes each slot visible before its counter moves.

screens.title: The full ring
screens.prose: Some rings keep wrapped indexes and give up one slot to tell full from empty. A ring of 4 with growing counters has head 7 and tail 11.
screens.question: How many items does it hold?

widget.accept: 4: the counters differ by 4, a full ring. Wrapped indexes would both read 3.

hints.text: Subtract the head from the tail.
Look at both counters in the ring of 4: slots 7 & 3 and 11 & 3.
$11 - 7 = 4$, and both slots are 3.

feedback.correct: 4: full, and every slot in use.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the head from the tail.

byKey.zero: The two slots are equal, but the counters differ by 4. That is full, not empty.
byKey.three: Counters let all four slots hold items. Only wrapped indexes would stop at three.

explain.text: The counters differ by 4, so all four slots are in use. Wrapped indexes would give 3 for both, and full would look like empty. Counters tell them apart, so a ring of $N$ holds $N$ items.

screens.title: Two counters that only grow
screens.question: When is the ring full?

options.why: Equal counters mean empty. Full is a gap of N.

options.text: When the head and tail slots are equal
options.why: Equal slots happen when empty and when full, so they cannot tell the two apart.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the counters, not the slots.

byKey.eq: Equal counters mean there is nothing in the ring.
byKey.slot: Both empty and full give equal slots.

explain.text: The mask turns a counter into a slot, and the difference of the counters says how many items wait. Unsigned subtraction stays right across the wrap, because $2^{32}$ is a multiple of $N$.

screens.title: Write the ring
screens.prose: Now the ring of ints. `push` returns false when full and `pop(out)` returns false when empty. Keep `head_` and `tail_` on separate cache lines: a test compares their addresses.

lines: push: false if tail_ - head_ == N
head_ and tail_ at least 64 bytes apart
params.title: The contract

screens.question: Fix `push` so the ring holds all `N` items, and put each counter on its own line.

widget.how: Ten hidden tests drive the ring with pushes and pops: full, empty, a capacity of 1 and many laps. One checks that the counters are 64 bytes apart.

hints.text: The ring may hold `N` items, not `N - 1`.
The full test is `tail_ - head_ == buf_.size()`.
Put `alignas(64)` before each of `head_` and `tail_`.

feedback.correct: That's it. Counters, a mask, and a line each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: The starter refuses a push one slot early, which loses an item. The exact test is tail minus head equal to the capacity. `alignas(64)` puts each counter at the start of its own line, so the two cores stop trading one.

screens.title: Drill: the ring by hand
screens.prose: Drill: about two minutes each. Say the reasoning aloud first. A push returns 1 when accepted and 0 when full. A pop returns the value, or -1 when empty.
screens.question: Fill in each answer.

rows: Ring of 1: push 7, then push 8. The second answer
The same ring: the next pop returns
Slot of counter 45 in a ring of 16 (45 & 15)
Items stored with head 100 and tail 103

hints.text: A ring of 1 holds one item.
$45 = 2 \times 16 + 13$. And tail minus head counts the items.
0, 7, 13 and 3. A mask costs one instruction, a division tens of cycles on many CPUs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: The ring of 1 is already full, so the push is refused.
byKey.r1c1: The first item pushed is the first popped.

explain.text: A ring of 1 is full after one push, so push 8 returns 0 and the pop returns 7. A mask finds the slot in one instruction where a modulo needs a division. Items stored is always the tail minus the head.

screens.title: Follow-up: size the ring
screens.prose: The interviewer asks you to size the ring. A consumer stall of 1 ms must lose nothing at 200,000 messages a second. A message is 24 bytes, and the capacity must be a power of two.
screens.question: Fill in the sizes.

rows: Slots for a 5 ms stall at 1,000,000 a second

hints.text: A millisecond at 200,000 a second is 200 messages.
Round up to the next power of two. Then multiply by 24.
200 messages, 256 slots, 6,144 bytes. And 5,000 messages round up to 8,192.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: 256 is the first power of two above 200.

explain.text: 200 messages round up to 256 slots, 6,144 bytes, which sits in L1. A 5 ms stall at a million a second needs 5,000 messages: 8,192 slots, 192 KiB, in L2. Say which stall the ring covers.

ideas: A ring of N slots, N a power of two, has two growing counters. Slot = counter & (N - 1), full when tail - head == N.
Powers of two keep slot order across a 32-bit wrap. A ring of 3 puts two counters in one slot.
One writer per counter needs no lock; give head and tail lines of their own with alignas(64).

formula.name: The ring
formula.note: N a power of two; full when the size is N.

summary.trap: Putting both counters on one cache line, so two cores trade it.

quiz.prose: A ring of 16 has head 37 and tail 50.
quiz.question: How many items does it hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the head counter from the tail counter.

byKey.slot: 2 is the next slot, 50 & 15. The question asks for the item count.

explain.text: The counters differ by $50 - 37 = 13$, so 13 items are stored. The next push goes to slot $50 \,\&\, 15 = 2$.

quiz.prose: A ring uses `counter & (N - 1)` for its slot.
quiz.question: Why must `N` be a power of two?

options.text: `N - 1` is all one bits, so `&` acts like `% N`
A power of two makes each push faster by itself
options.why: Speed comes from the mask replacing a division. Other sizes break the mask.

options.text: So the ring fills exactly one cache line
options.why: The ring is far larger than a line. The reason is the mask.

options.text: So the head and tail never meet
options.why: They meet when empty and when full. The size does not change that.

feedback.correct: The mask works only for a power of two.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does `N - 1` look like in binary?

byKey.fast: The mask is quick only when it gives the right answer.

explain.text: For $N = 8$, `& 7` keeps the low three bits, which is the remainder mod 8. For $N = 6$, the mask 101 would keep the wrong bits.

quiz.prose: A consumer may stall for 5 ms. The feed sends 400,000 messages a second, and the ring size must be a power of two.
quiz.question: How many slots does the ring need?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the messages in the stall, then round up to a power of two.

byKey.raw: 2,000 messages is the stall. A power of two is needed, so round up.

explain.text: 5 ms at 400,000 a second is 2,000 messages. The next power of two is $2^{11} = 2{,}048$.

quiz.prose: In a single-producer, single-consumer ring, a thread writes `head_` and a thread writes `tail_`.
quiz.question: Which thread writes `head_`?

options.why: The producer reads `head_` to check for room. It writes `tail_`.
Two writers would need a lock. The design gives each counter one writer.

options.text: Neither: the counter is read only
options.why: Popping moves the head, so the consumer writes it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which thread removes items?

byKey.both: Each counter has a single writer.
byKey.neither: Every pop adds one to the head.

explain.text: A pop removes an item and adds one to `head_`, so the consumer is its only writer. The producer owns `tail_` and only reads `head_`.
